Q: using isinf() on IRIX-6.5 A:

The compiler is rather old (GCC-3.3), but it should support C99 just fine, ...

Yet GCC 3.3 offers a large, but limited C99 features.

My thinking is that that compiler is not fully compliant in the math.h area for OP.

int isinf(real-floating x); was added in C99. Prior to that various compilers may have offered a similar function of macro.

generic was added in C11. Prior to that various compilers used a similar, yet internal, generic concept to employ: int isinf(real-floating x);

I would expect strict C99 usage (like -std=c99) should work.

Usage with a compiler extension C99 -std=gnu99 may work. Yet that is what OP is claiming does not.

Some things to try, which may help:

  • Add #include <tgmath.h>.

Some things to try, yet I expect them to fail likewise:

  • Try -std=c99.

  • Try float f = 42.; int x = isinf((double)f);.

A hacky C89 to C23 alternative:

  int x = (f == f) && (f > FLT_MAX || f < -FLT_MAX);

This technically has some NAN issues as when f is a NAN in the above is not C specified to behave as hoped, yet usually does.

Steering code with #if __STDC_VERSION__ >= 199901 may be problematic for GCC 3.3.

Q: How to print Unicode character in C++ A:

This has gotten some useful answers, but there are still some aspects I’m surprised no one has covered.

Wide Streams

According to the Standard, std::wcout is supposed to be a std::basic_ostream<wchar_t> that works like std::cout but for wide characters. There’s similarly std::wcin and std::werr. The following is supposed to work:

wchar_t f = L'\u0444';
wcout << f << endl;

In practice, this will compile everywhere, but won’t work consistently on Windows without a bit of extra initialization, and Linux is finicky about using both wide and narrow streams in the same program.

Wide-Character Strings

Mixing output to wcout or wprintf() with cout or printf() doesn’t work reliably, and the standard library disables wide-character output to cout and std::print(). However, printf() can print wide strings with a format specifier of %ls and wide characters with a format specifier of %lc—if the locale and console are properly configured.

The wchar_t type is not really portable. The C and C++ standards specified that wchar_t must be a fixed-width encoding round-trip convertible with every character in every supported locale. All the string-processing functions in the standard library operate on the assumption that it is. Microsoft originally took the Unicode Consortium’s word that 16 bits would be enough forever. Then, when the Consortium realized that 65,536 characters would not be enough for round-trip compatibility with all the character sets they wanted, and retroactively made UTF-16 a variable-width encoding, Microsoft refused to break backward compatibility with every Windows program in existence. Then it introduced locales that need to use characters that need UTF-16 surrogate pairs, such as Chinese and Japanese. So Windows now defines wchar_t as UTF-16, where some Unicode codepoints are encoded as surrogate pairs..

Linux compilers, on the other hand, chose to make wchar_t a fixed-width 32-bit type. The wide-character string functions are there but almost never used. A char* is now almost always assumed to be in UTF-8.

All C++ compilers support char8_t, char16_6 and char32_t. However, the only support for them in the standard library is some deprecated functions to convert between these encodings. Practical Unicode text processing uses some third-party library like ICU or Boost.

Portably Encoding UTF-8 Strings

In practical, real-world use, you want to output UTF-8, and probably store your strings in UTF-8 as well. The standard way since C17 to encode this as a UTF-8 constant is:

static constexpr char efBytes[] = u8"\u0444";

This is specified to get you an array with the UTF-8 bytes {0xD1, 0x84, 0x00} no matter what your source character set and execution character set are configured to. This will come in handy when you cannot configure the entire build system to use UTF-8. Whenever possible, a codebase should store source code as UTF-8 (and saving with a BOM can help some compilers detect this unambiguously). That lets you write:

static constexpr char efBytes[] = u8"ф";

Either way, I normally turn this char array into a std::string_view:

static constexpr std::string_view efSV{efBytes};

If this isn’t an option, I at least want the length as a compile-time constant:

static constexpr auto efLength = sizeof(efBytes) - 1U; // Minus terminating null.

Compilers do need both constexpr and static to get full optimization of these string constants. Modern compilers will now do constant-folding on the string and its size, at compile time. {If you declare it globally at file scope, of course, it’s automatically static storage class and the static keyword only controls its visibility in other source files.)

If you also configure the compiler to use UTF-8 as the execution character set, the u8" prefix should not be necessary. Modern C++ does not support mixing u8" literals (of type char8_t*) with char-oriented strings and streams. For example, cout << u8"ф"; does not work. (Ths is a breaking change from C++17.) If you are on a compiler where cout << "\u0444"; does not work reliably either, your best option is to store the bytes in a named char array and output that. In some contexts, (char*)u8"\u0444" would work.

Setting up UTF-8 on Windows

On current builds of Windows 10 and 11 (and when linking to the Universal CRT on earlier versions it supports), there are a few steps you want to take:

  • Set compiler flags in the build script to use UTF-8 as the source and execution character set (which should be /utf-8 for MSVC or the default on Clang or GCC)
  • Set the process activeCodePage to UTF-8 in the app manifest
  • At start-up, call std::locale::global(std::locale{".UTF-8"}); to set the current C/C++ locale to the default language and the character set to UTF-8. Or choose a specific language, such as "en_US.UTF-8".
  • Call SetConsoleCP(CP_UTF8) and SetConsoleOutputCP(CP_UTF8) to put the console in UTF-8 mode.
  • Some Windows functions (like FormatMessage) may still check the thread-preferred language list rather than the current locale, and need you to call SetThreadPreferredUILanguages(), or else to save the language ID in a global variable
  • You may need to set CMD.EXE (or your other terminal program) to a monospace Unicode font, such as Lucida Console.

You may in some situations need to use the wide-character API for compatibility with systems that set the global encoding to something other than UTF-8. For example, if you are using GUI functions rather than console mode, the Windows documentation warns,

Windows graphics device interface (GDI) doesn't currently support setting the activeCodePage property per process. Instead, GDI defaults to the active system codepage.

The fwide() standard library call exists on Windows, but does not do anything.

The Windows terminal does not correctly display right-to-left scripts, even if you insert LTR/RTL codes manually. You would need to manually find the grapheme boundaries and print the graphemes in reverse order.

On Linux

All commonly-used distributions use UTF-8 locales exclusively. However, C++ programs still start up in the "C" locale, so you want to switch to the user-selected locale with

std::locale::global(std::locale{""})

or in some cases the default English locale with

std::locale::global(std::locale{"en_US.UTF-8"})

Setting the C++ locale also sets the C locale, so you do not also need to call setlocale(LC_ALL, "").

Obsolete character sets from the ’90s are still supported. Since it is possible for the environment to be configured so that setting the locale to "" selects an encoding other than UTF-8, and the available locales and their names may vary, you can check this with

strcmp(nl_langinfo(CODESET), "UTF-8") == 0

Linux terminal programs now all support UTF-8, and if they ever need to drop back to a legacy character set, emulate that through something like luit. The Linux text-mode console would need to load a console driver and a bitmap font, currently limited to 256 or 512 characters.

It is possible to put stdout or another file in wide-character mode on Linux by calling fwide(). Wide characters on Linux are 32-bit and a fixed-width encoding. The standard-library and POSIX wide-character-handling routines are not adequate for many purposes, but at least they work.

Several other text-mode libraries support UTF-8 or wide characters, including ncurses (since 2002).

Q: org.apache.openejb.config.ValidationFailedException: Module failed validation. AppModule(name=appname) TomEE A:

The message really describes wide variety of meanings. In my case there it has been written in log-file and nothing more distinct except "SEVERE [main] org.apache.openejb.config.ReportValidationResults.logResults ERROR ... null: Cannot validate jar: ...". But in console there was more clear notice "java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: ..." So check logs and console together.

Q: How to config and lookup JNDI in websphere? A:

When you create an EJB project in Eclipse, an EJB deployment descriptor is created. You have to add all your JNDI resources in it, in the references tab. And you have to add websphere runtime JARs same as you have added any other JARs.

Q: POST form data using WinInet c++ A:

Your code is nearly correct, you must make sure of the following points:

  1. char* hdrs="Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded"; you must make sure that your return object from POST message will be of type x-www-form-urlencoded or JSON . if it's JSON you need to define char* hdrs="Content-Type: application/json\r\n"; Note: you must append \r\n to the hdrs.

  2. try to call readFile method with buffer of size 10000 for example and print buffer , it will print the output of the response to the connection

  3. In HINTERNET hRequest2 = HttpOpenRequest(hConnect, "POST","/", NULL, NULL, accept, 0, 0); instead of "/" you must call the path of the requested API for example: .
    In HINTERNET hRequest2 = HttpOpenRequest(hConnect, "POST", "/users/jsonlogin", NULL, NULL, accept, 0, 0);

Q: LinQ & DataTable Group By in C# A:

There is no unique item in your group but you can select the first item and show the fields:

    select 
    new { StockCardCode = grp.Key, 
    Quantity = grp.Sum(r => r.Field<decimal>("Quantity")),
    Explain = grp.First().Select(x=>x.Field<string>("Explain"))}
